title: Quantum Decision Theory for Displacement Detection with Finite-Energy GKP States
abstract: We develop a quantum-decision-theoretic framework for detecting phase-space displacements with finite-energy, $d$-level Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) probes. For single-mode and entanglement-assisted architectures, we derive the Bayesian minimum-error probability, the optimal Neyman-Pearson receiver-operating characteristic, and the corresponding minimum detectable displacement. Finite-energy effects are treated through exact theta-series displacement kernels, while pure loss followed by quantum-limited amplification is mapped to an effective Gaussian random-displacement channel. Entanglement removes preparation-dependent blind directions and preserves both logical displacement labels, although it does not surpass the pointwise optimized single-mode strategy in the noiseless pure-state setting. We benchmark the resulting protocols against coherent-state, direction-matched squeezed-vacuum, and twin-beam schemes at equal nominal squeezing. Numerical results identify finite-squeezing and lossy regimes in which GKP probes achieve both a lower Bayesian error and a smaller minimum detectable perturbation than the selected Gaussian receivers.
summary: This paper establishes a rigorous decision-theoretic framework to detect phase-space displacements using finite-energy GKP states. It derives optimal detection metrics by comparing GKP performance against standard Gaussian probes under realistic loss and amplification noise channels. The key finding is that GKP encoding offers superior sensing capabilities in specific noisy regimes compared to purely Gaussian approaches.
main_problem: The paper develops a quantum-decision-theoretic framework to determine if an unknown phase-space displacement has occurred using finite-energy Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) probes.
main_result: Under lossy and finite-squeezing regimes, GKP probes can achieve lower Bayesian error probabilities and detect smaller displacements compared to optimized Gaussian receivers.
method: The authors employ quantum decision theory metrics (Bayesian minimum-error probability and Neyman-Pearson ROC) applied to bosonic systems undergoing displacement channels.
model_or_system: The system models a single bosonic mode subjected to unknown phase-space displacements, analyzed using finite-energy GKP states as probes. The analysis incorporates realistic noise channels like pure loss followed by quantum-limited amplification.
key_observables: Bayesian error probability ($P_e^\star$), Neyman-Pearson receiver operating characteristic ($p_{11}(p_{10})$), and the minimum detectable displacement.
important_parameters: Finite squeezing level, logical dimension ($d$), channel transmissivity ($\eta$), and amplification gain ($G$).
main_assumptions: The analysis treats pure loss followed by quantum-limited amplification as an effective Gaussian random-displacement channel; entanglement does not surpass the single-mode optimum in noiseless pure states.
figures_summary: Figure 5 compares ROC curves and minimum detectable displacement thresholds for GKP vs. Gaussian protocols under varying transmissivity, showing performance advantages for GKP in specific regimes.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the decision theory framework, derives optimal metrics using characteristic functions, models loss/amplification channels, analyzes single-mode versus entanglement-assisted GKP sensing, and concludes with numerical comparisons against Gaussian benchmarks.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses quantum metrology limits by analyzing non-Gaussian probes (GKP states) in realistic noisy environments (lossy channels), which is crucial for practical quantum sensing applications beyond the ideal vacuum case.
